interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is only about 37% of the fifty units still on the shelf when you drag Years in service to the MTBF of 10 years.
interactive.title: The shelf of units
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens. Simulated units are drawn as beads on a shelf. Each bead is one unit in service, say a pump. Every unit has the same steady failure rate, λ. Here it is 0.1 a year, as an example. A rule on screen gives each unit a random lifetime: t = −ln(u) ÷ λ. Here u is a random number between 0 and 1. That rule gives every unit the same steady rate at every age. A slider, Years in service, runs from 0 to 30 years in steps of 1 year. It opens at 5. As it moves, a clock's hand runs. Each unit drops off the shelf when its lifetime runs out. It lands on a beam marked in years. So the fallen units pile up by the year they failed. A curve over the pile shows what the rule expects. A dashed line marks the MTBF, 10 years. Under the years, a strip draws the failure rate of the units still working. Tiles sit below the strip. Still working counts the units on the shelf. The rule expects gives 50 × e^(−λt). Another tile gives the MTBF. Failure rate now gives the rate per year for each unit still working. On the bathtub it gives the sketch's rate at that age. A choice, Units, offers One by one, Pairs in series and Pairs in parallel. In pairs, the fifty units make 25 pairs. A pair in series stops at its first failure. A pair in parallel stops at its second. Its failed unit stays on the shelf, held by its partner. A last view, The bathtub, draws each unit's failure rate from a sketch. Say it starts with an early extra 0.25 a year that fades over about a year. Under that sits a steady 0.02 a year. Wear-out then climbs steeply near 24 years. Its slider runs the clock from 0 to 30 years. It opens at 30. The screens. 1, show: fifty units sit on a shelf. Each drops off when it fails. Drag Years in service. Units drop as the clock runs. The strip below reads flat at 0.1 a year. That is the failure rate: failures each year for each unit still working. Here an old unit is as likely to fail next month as a new one. The shelf empties fastest at first only because more units are there to fail. Its finished picture shows 5 years in service, with the strip flat. 2, a puzzle: at 5 years, say 30 units are still working. About how many fail in the next year? Offered: about 3; about 5; and about 1, as the weak ones have already gone. Hint when wrong: the rate counts failures for each unit still working. Here it does not change with age. 3, show: the share still working is the reliability, R. Each short spell, the shelf loses the same fraction of what is left. That gives the decay curve you know from a capacitor: R = e^(−λt). At 5 years, R = e^(−0.5), about 0.61. So the rule expects 30.3 of the fifty. MTBF means mean time between failures. A unit fails 0.1 times for each year it runs. So on average it runs 1 ÷ λ = 10 years to a failure. A dashed line marks it. Its finished picture shows 5 years in service with the rule's curve over the pile. 4, a puzzle: the MTBF here is 10 years. At 10 years in service, what share of the units still work? Offered: about 37%; about half; and nearly all, as 10 years is their mean life. Hint: put t = 10 into R = e^(−0.1t). 5, show: slide to 10 years. The shelf holds close to the 18.4 the rule expects. That is about 37%, the same 0.37 you meet after one time constant. Most units fail before the mean lifetime. A few long-lived units pull the mean up. A long high tail did the same with insulation resistance. Half have failed by about 7 years. So the MTBF is a rate turned over, not a life to count on. Its finished picture shows 10 years in service at the MTBF line. 6, a puzzle: λ is 0.1 a year. What is the chance one unit has failed by 5 years? Offered: about 39%; about 61%; and 50%, as 5 years is half the MTBF. Hint: R is the chance it still works. So the chance it has failed is 1 − R. 7, show: choose Pairs in series. A pair works only while both units work. A share R of the first units still works. R of those have a working partner. If each unit fails on its own, R × R of pairs still work. That is e^(−2λt). So the rates add to 0.2 a year. The shelf empties twice as fast. The MTBF halves to 5 years. Working case: both work. Failing case: either fails. Its finished picture shows pairs in series at 10 years, about 13.5% left. 8, a puzzle: a pump and its starter are in series. Each has a 0.9 chance of lasting the year. What is the chance the pair lasts the year? Offered: 0.81; 1.8; and 0.9, the chance of each part. Hint: both must last, so take 0.9 of 0.9. 9, show: choose Pairs in parallel. A pair works while at least one unit works. So work the failing case: both fail with chance (1 − R) × (1 − R). The pair's reliability is 1 − (1 − R)², about 60% at 10 years. The failure rate starts at zero, because one failure leaves a pair working. Two units run, so the first failure comes after 5 years on average. The survivor then runs another 10 on average. So the MTBF is 15 years. Its finished picture shows pairs in parallel at 10 years, the rate climbing. 10, a puzzle: two battery chargers run in parallel. Each has a 0.9 chance of lasting the year. What is the chance at least one lasts? Offered: 0.99; 0.81; and 0.18, one working and the other not. Hint: the pair fails only if both fail. Find that chance, then take it from 1. 11, show: real units are rarely steady for life. Units with hidden faults often fail early, so the rate starts high. For most of a useful life it settles low and roughly steady. Then wear-out sets in, and the rate climbs. That shape is the bathtub curve. This one is a sketch, not measured. The steady model fits only its flat middle. Its finished picture shows the clock run to 30 years: an early heap, a quiet floor and a wear-out hump under the sketched rate. 12, a puzzle: say two units sit in the flat middle of their lives. One has run 8 years, the other 3. Which is more likely to fail next year? Offered: the same chance for both; the 8-year unit, as it is older; and the 3-year unit, as the older one has proved itself. Hint: in the flat middle, the rate does not change with age. 13, a mixed puzzle: an example UPS has a rectifier, a battery and an inverter in series. Say their failure rates are 20, 10 and 20 per million hours. What is the UPS's MTBF? Offered: 20,000 hours; 50,000 hours, the weakest part's; and 200,000 hours, the parts' MTBFs added. Hint: in series, any failure stops it. So the failure rates add. Then turn the total over. 14, a mixed puzzle: two UPSs run in parallel from one shared battery bank. Is 1 − (1 − R)² right for the pair? Offered: no, too hopeful, as a battery fault can stop both; yes, as parallel pairs always work that way; and no, it should be R × R. Hint: the parallel rule assumes each unit fails on its own. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a narrow phone, the tiles and answers wrap onto more lines. No word ever splits.
interactive.ignores: The units are simulated from the rules on screen, not taken from real equipment. The failure rate of 0.1 a year and the bathtub's shape are examples. The clock runs years in seconds. With only fifty units, the shelf's count wanders a little either side of what the rule expects. Here each unit in a pair fails wholly on its own. Real pairs share a supply, a room and the same wear. The pair rules leave that out. The bathtub is a sketch, not a model fitted to real failures. A failed unit is simply gone here. In real service it is repaired or replaced.

explain.text:
Units of the same kind do not all fail at the same age. Each fails at its own random time. A [[failure rate]] says how often they fail. It counts failures each year, or each hour, for each unit still working. If all goes well, that rate stays roughly steady for most of a product's useful life.[^1] A steady rate sets the share of units still working at any age. It also means far fewer reach the average lifetime than you might expect.

Here is why. Call the rate λ. Over a short spell, every working unit has the same small chance of failing. That chance is λ times the spell. So the stock loses the same fraction of what is left in every spell. That gives the decay curve you met with a capacitor discharging. The share still working is the [[reliability]], R = e^(−λt). One over the rate, 1 ÷ λ, is the mean time to failure. In power work it is usually called the [[MTBF]], the mean time between failures.[^2] Say a unit fails 0.1 times for each year it runs. Then on average it runs 10 years to a failure. Put t = 1 ÷ λ into the rule, and R = e^(−1), about 0.37. Most lifetimes pile up at the short end. A long tail of units lasts far longer. That tail pulls the mean up, so most units fail before the mean. Yet at 0.1 a year, half have failed by about 7 years.

Pairs of units follow two rules, as long as each unit fails on its own. In series, the pair works only while both work. A share R of the first units still works. A share R of those have a working partner. So the pair's R is R × R. That is e^(−λt) × e^(−λt) = e^(−2λt). So the failure rates add. In parallel, the pair works while at least one works. It fails only if both fail, with chance (1 − R) × (1 − R). So its R is 1 − (1 − R)². A part the two share, such as one supply, can stop both at once. Then the parallel rule promises too much.

Real units are rarely steady for their whole lives. Units with hidden faults often fail early. Late in life, wear-out makes the rate climb. That shape is called the bathtub curve. The steady model fits only its flat middle. There a failure comes by chance, not age. A climbing rate means wear. A rising Zs asks the same of a reading: real wear, or scatter?

**With a steady failure rate λ, the share of units still working after a time t is e^(−λt). So only about 37% reach the MTBF of 1 ÷ λ.[^3]**

analogy.text: Think of a capacitor discharging through a resistor. Its voltage falls by the same fraction in each equal slice of time. After one time constant, RC, about 37% is left. A stock of units with a steady failure rate empties the same way. The MTBF plays the part of RC. So after one MTBF, about 37% are still working.
analogy.breaks: Charge drains smoothly, all of it alike. Units fail one at a time, at random. So at the MTBF, fifty units land a few either side of the 18.4 the rule expects. A capacitor also follows its curve all the way down. Real units keep a steady rate only through the flat middle of their lives.

practice.text:
- Find the failure rate or the MTBF, and note its units: per hour, per million hours or per year.
- Check that the kit sits in the flat middle of its life. New kit and worn kit often fail faster.
- Work the share still working at your time with R = e^(−λt). The chance it has failed is 1 − R.
- For parts in series, add the failure rates, or multiply the R's.
- For parts in parallel, find the chance they all fail, then take it from 1.
- Look for anything a parallel pair shares, such as one supply or one switch. A shared part sits in series with the pair.
- Keep testing standby kit. A figure on paper cannot show that this unit will start today.

**Rules of thumb:** at the MTBF, about 37% are still working. At half the MTBF, about 61% are. At a tenth of it, about 90% are.

**Worked example:** take the example UPS. Its parts sit in series, with failure rates of 20, 10 and 20 per million hours. They add to 50 per million hours. So the MTBF is 20,000 hours. That sounds like more than two years of running. Now run it for one year, 8760 hours. Then λt = 50 × 8760 ÷ 1,000,000, about 0.44. R = e^(−0.44), about 0.65. So about one such unit in three would fail within a year's running. Add a second UPS in parallel, with nothing shared. Both fail with chance (1 − R)², about 0.13. So the pair keeps the load with a chance of about 0.87.

**Standby kit:** a standby generator in its useful life can be modelled with a steady failure rate while it runs.[^4] It must also start when called. That is a separate chance. A running failure rate leaves it out.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the MTBF as how long each unit lasts.
- Expecting half the units to reach the MTBF.
- Adding reliabilities in series instead of multiplying them.
- Counting only "one works and the other not" for a parallel pair.
- Using the parallel rule on units that share a part.
- Using a steady rate for brand-new or worn-out kit.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is only about 37% of the fifty units still on the shelf when you drag Years in service to the MTBF of 10 years.

checks.label: Only 36.7% of units are statistically likely to operate as long as the MTBF: with R(t) = e^(−λt), R at the MTBF of 1 ÷ λ is e^(−1) = 0.368, and of 20,000 lifetimes from the rule on screen at λ = 0.1 a year, about 36.8% outlast 10 years
The inverse of λ, 1/λ, gives the mean time to failure, the MTBF: at λ = 0.1 a year that is 10 years, and 20,000 lifetimes from the rule on screen average about 10 years

Worked by hand: 30 × 0.1 = 3 and 50 × 0.1 = 5; e^(−0.5) = 0.61, so 50 × e^(−0.5) = 30.3 and 1 − e^(−0.5) = 39%; 50 × e^(−1) = 18.4, 37%; ln 2 ÷ 0.1 = 6.9, about 7 years; in series e^(−2) = 13.5%, 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 a year and an MTBF of 5 years; in parallel 1 − (1 − e^(−1))² = 60%, and R added up over all time gives an MTBF of 15 years; 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, 1 − 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.99 and 0.9 × 0.1 + 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.18; 20 + 10 + 20 = 50 per million hours, so 1,000,000 ÷ 50 = 20,000 hours, the weakest part alone 50,000 and the MTBFs added 200,000. From the batch shown: 30 of 50 still work at 5 years, 27 at 6, 25 at 7 and 18 at 10; in series 21 of 25 pairs at 1 year and 3 at 10; in parallel all 25 at 1 year and 15 at 10

Shapes the rules give: one unit's failure rate is flat at 0.1 a year at every age and a series pair's at 0.2, while a parallel pair's starts at 0 and climbs towards 0.1 without reaching it; a steady rate loses the same share of what is left each year; the bathtub sketch starts high, sits near 0.02 a year in its middle years and climbs past 0.3 with wear-out; its batch fails in an early heap, a quiet floor and a wear-out hump; a lifetime is where the failure rate added up reaches −ln u

Drawn right, and each puzzle hidden until answered: every unit stays on the picture at full size; each puzzle accepts one right answer of three, and before it nothing gives the answer away (the clock waits, no dots on the rate, no rates added, no fault); a right answer brings each in; every demonstration settles within 5 s and every answer within 2.5 s

applied.problem: 0.35 × 0.35 is 0.1225, which rounds to 0.12, not 0.13; 0.13 only comes from the unrounded 0.355. Also one study that assumes a steady running rate for its generators does not show it is "usually" modelled that way.
"near 18" is a number outside the numbers list and understates the spread: fifty random units typically land several either side of 18.4 (spread about 3), as the ignores panel says.
Defining a failure rate as failures "each year" reads as if that were its only unit; real figures are often per hour or per million hours, as the practice and worked example use.
